Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm in which a program is organised as a collection of objects that work together. Each object bundles the data that describes it with the subroutines that act on that data, so a hire bike in a city bike-share system knows its own identifier, dock and battery level and also knows how to record a ride. This contrasts with a procedural program, where data is usually held in separate variables or records and passed into free-standing procedures and functions. The central ideas are the class, which acts as the template, and the object, which is a specific thing built from that template.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Classes are made robust by encapsulation: their data is kept private and can only be reached through the methods the class chooses to make public. OOP became popular because large systems are easier to build, test and maintain when they are divided into self-contained classes that mirror real-world entities such as customers, accounts, tickets or buses. This lesson covers classes, objects, attributes, methods, parameter lists, constructors, encapsulation with get and set methods and properties, and class diagrams, using C sharp throughout.
Right. What else do we need to know?

A class is a template, or blueprint, that defines what every object of a particular type will contain: its attributes (the data it stores) and its methods (the behaviours it can perform). By convention a class name begins with a capital letter, for example Bike, Book or Patient. An object is one specific instance of a class. Two Bike objects share exactly the same list of attributes and the same method code, but each holds its own values, so one may be docked at City Hall with 80 percent charge while another sits at Titanic Quarter with 35 percent.
Got it. Keep going.

The set of values held in an object's attributes at any moment is called its state. Creating an object is called instantiation, and in C sharp it is done with the new keyword, as in Bike b1 equals new Bike(BK101, City Hall, 80);. The variable b1 holds a reference to the new object, and its methods are then called with dot notation, such as b1.Ride(12, Queen's University). One class can be used to create any number of objects, which is why a well-designed class saves so much repeated code: a school library needs one Book class, not thousands of separate sets of variables.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Attributes, which some books call properties or fields, are variables declared inside a class. Each needs a suitable data type: a bike's ID is a string, its battery percentage is an integer, a hire price is a real number and whether a bike is reserved is a Boolean. Methods are subroutines declared inside a class that describe what an object can do or what can be done to it; the textbook also calls them behaviours. A method header shows its access modifier, return type, name and parameter list.
Okay. Keep going.

The parameter list states what extra information the method needs to do its job, giving a type and a name for each item, so SetDock(string newDock) must be given a string, such as Botanic, every time it is called. A method that needs no extra information has an empty parameter list, written as a pair of empty brackets, as in GetBattery. The return type is void if the method simply carries out an action, or a data type such as int or string if it sends a value back to the calling code. The values actually supplied in a call are called arguments, and they must match the parameters in number, order and type.
Go on.

A constructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is instantiated, and its job is to give the new object a sensible starting state. In C sharp a constructor has exactly the same name as its class and no return type at all, not even void, which is how it can be recognised in code and in class diagrams. Its parameters usually supply initial values that are copied into the private attributes, for example public Bike(string id, string startDock, int charge). If a parameter has the same name as an attribute, the keyword this identifies the attribute, as in this dot name equals name;.
Right. Keep going.

If a programmer writes no constructor at all, C sharp supplies a default one with no parameters, which leaves attributes at default values such as 0, false or null. A class may have more than one constructor provided their parameter lists differ, letting objects be created with different amounts of starting information. Constructors are also the natural place to set attributes that must never change afterwards, such as a membership number: the value is assigned once when the object is built and, because no set method is provided, it stays fixed for the life of the object.
Go on.

Encapsulation means combining an object's data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, the class, and hiding the internal details so that the data can only be read or changed through methods the class provides. In C sharp the attributes are declared private, which stops code outside the class accessing them directly. Public get methods, or getters, return the current value of an attribute, and public set methods, or setters, change it. This gives the class control over every change. A setter can validate the new value, for instance rejecting a negative age, so an object can never be put into an invalid state.
Makes sense. Keep going.

An attribute that should never change once it has been allocated, such as a National Insurance number or a hospital number, is given a getter but no setter, which makes it read-only. A setter can also carry out related tasks, such as recording a change of address in an audit log, so programmers who use the class do not have to remember those side effects every time. Because other code depends only on the public methods, the internal storage can later be redesigned without breaking the rest of the program. C sharp properties provide the same controlled access in a more compact form.
Go on.

A class diagram is a design notation, taken from the Unified Modelling Language (UML), that shows a class as a rectangle divided into three compartments. The top compartment holds the class name, the middle compartment lists the attributes with their data types, and the bottom compartment lists the methods with their parameters and return types, for example plus Ride(minutes: int, endDock: string): void. Visibility is shown by a symbol in front of each member: a minus sign for private, a plus sign for public and a hash for protected. In a well-encapsulated class most attributes carry a minus sign, while the methods that form the public interface carry a plus sign.
Got it. Keep going.

The constructor is listed among the methods, with the class's name and no return type. Class diagrams are drawn during design, before coding, so that a team can agree what each class will store and do and how the classes relate to one another, and they then serve as documentation for anyone maintaining the program later. Books and papers vary slightly in style, for instance writing 'return int' instead of ': int', so what matters is that names, data types and visibility are clear and consistent.

What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Definitions are a reliable source of marks when both halves are present. A class is a template or blueprint that defines the attributes and methods (behaviours) of a type of object; an object is a specific instance of a class with its own attribute values. Questions that say 'by referring to the code' expect you to name the actual class, objects, attributes and methods from the listing, so quote identifiers such as Bike, b1, battery or Ride rather than giving only a general definition. For encapsulation, a full answer says that data and methods are held together in the class, that the attributes are made private, and that they can only be accessed or changed through get and set methods. When you write a class, examiners look for private attributes with sensible data types, a constructor that assigns every parameter to an attribute, getters that return values, setters that take a parameter and return nothing, and a display method if one is asked for. Watch for attributes that must not change, such as a student or membership number, and give them no setter. In output questions, work through each statement in order and copy the spaces, punctuation and line breaks exactly. A common slip is giving a constructor a return type.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A Patient class has a private attribute hospitalNumber with a get method but no set method. What is the effect? Is it A, Other code can never see the hospital number; B, The program will not compile without a setter; C, Other code can read the hospital number but cannot change it; D, Any code can change the hospital number directly?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: Other code can read the hospital number but cannot change it. A getter alone makes the attribute read-only from outside the class, which suits identifiers that must never change.
